AMD delivers record quarter as Data Center segment revenue grows 97% year-over-year, driven by record sales of AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) today announced financial results for the third quarter of 2026. Third quarter revenue was $13.4 billion, gross margin was 54%, operating income was $2.8 billion, net income was $2.4 billion and diluted earnings per share was $1.46. On a non-GAAP
(*)
basis, gross margin was 56%, operating income was $3.9 billion, net income was $3.5 billion and diluted earnings per share was $2.09.
“We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year,” said Dr. Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO. “Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and ‘Venice’ production. With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years.”
“Third quarter revenue grew 45% year-over-year to a record $13.4 billion, while non-GAAP earnings per share grew 74%, demonstrating the significant operating leverage in our business model as our Data Center business drives scale,” said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, chief financial officer and treasurer. “Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our Data Center portfolio.”

Data Center segment revenue was a record $8.5 billion, up 97% year-over-year, driven by strong demand for AMD EPYC™ processors and the launch of AMD Instinct™ MI450 Series GPUs.
Client and Gaming segment revenue was $3.7 billion, down 8% year-over-year. Client business revenue was $2.9 billion, up 7% year-over-year, driven by sales of AMD Ryzen™ mobile processors. Gaming business revenue was $773 million, down 40% year-over-year, due to lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.
Embedded segment revenue was $1.1 billion, up 29% year-over-year, led by growth in aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets.

Our mission
We build the foundation for understanding AI’s economic impact. The Anthropic Economic Index tracks how AI tools are being used around the world and across every sector of the economy. Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.
You can submit a
proposal for a project here
.
Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.
We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.
We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.
We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.
We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.
Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.
This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our
Life Sciences Verification Program
. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our
AI for Science initiative
, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

Monthly API credits for Max, Ultra, and Team plans
Updated this week
Copy for LLM
Max, Ultra, and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max
$100
Ultra
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max, Ultra, or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max or Ultra:
to be the subscriber
Team:
to be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max or Ultra subscriber, or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max to Ultra.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max or Ultra to Team.
Your Max or Ultra link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max, Ultra, or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with
-p
.

Claude Cowork and chat are one Claude
Updated this week
Copy for LLM
We’re introducing a new way to use both Claude Cowork and chat that removes the distinction between the two products: in the new experience, these are merged into a single conversation, so you don’t need to decide which option better suits your task before getting started. Ask Claude for what you need, and it can decide which tool to use. Claude can answer a quick question, and it can also take on more complex work, like research, reports, spreadsheets, and presentations, and hand it back as finished files you can edit. With the new Claude experience, you ask for all of it in the same conversation, with no mode to choose. What you could previously only do in Claude Cowork is available from any conversation.
The new Claude experience is rolling out gradually, starting with Pro, Max, and Ultra plans on web, desktop, and mobile. On Team plans (in beta) and Enterprise plans, it's available where
Chat and Cowork unified
is turned on.
Why you might not have it yet
We're rolling this new experience out in stages, so even accounts on the same plan will see the changes at different times. You don't need to do anything to enable the new experience. If you're on a Pro, Max, or Ultra plan and your message box still shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you don't have it yet. Until then, keep using chat and Claude Cowork as you do today, where you can do most of what's in this article. Your chats, tasks, projects, and settings come with you when your account moves over. Once your account has the new experience, you can't switch back to separate "Chat" and "Cowork" options.
What Claude can do
Hand Claude a whole task
Describe the outcome you want, and Claude works through the steps on its own: searching the web, reading your files, running code, and putting the results together. You don't need to break the work into steps or pick a mode first. A quick question still gets a quick answer, and you can have several tasks running at the same time.
Try: "Go through these five interview notes and pull out the top themes, with a quote for each."
Step away while Claude works
More involved tasks keep running in the cloud even if you close your laptop or leave the page. Come back when the task is done, and the result is waiting in the conversation. Tasks that use files or apps on your computer need Claude Desktop open.
Try: "Research the top project management tools for small teams and write up a comparison. I'll check back later."
Get finished files back
Claude can create documents, spreadsheets with working formulas, and presentations you can open in PowerPoint. Download them and use them anywhere, or ask Claude to keep refining them.
Try: "Turn this analysis into a 10-slide deck I can present on Monday."
Create designs, decks, and docs
Claude can build charts, diagrams, and interactive visuals right in the conversation. Learn more in
Custom visuals in chat and Cowork
. On paid plans, you can also ask for a design, deck, or doc for work you'll put in front of others. Claude Design makes on-brand visuals and mockups, Claude Slides makes presentations, and Claude Docs makes living documents you write with Claude and your team (Claude Design, Claude Slides, and Claude Docs are in beta.) Edit the result yourself or tell Claude what to change, then share it by link or export it. Learn more in
What are artifacts and how do I use them?
Try: "Make a one-page visual summary of this launch plan."
Use the apps you've connected
Apps you've connected to Claude (like Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft 365, or Slack) work while Claude carries out a task, so it can pull what it needs as it goes. Connect apps in
Customize > Connectors
.
Try: "Find last quarter's board deck in my Drive and summarize what changed since."
Work on the web and on your computer
Files and folders:
In Claude Desktop, give Claude access to a folder on your computer so it can read, organize, and create files there.
Browsing:
Claude can open sites, read pages, click, and fill in forms, using the browser built into Claude Desktop or your own Chrome browser through Claude in Chrome. Learn more in
Use the built-in browser in Claude Cowork
.
Computer use:
In beta on Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, Claude can use apps on your computer directly by clicking, typing, and navigating your screen. Learn more in
Let Claude use your computer in Cowork
.
Claude reaches your local files, the built-in browser, and computer use only while Claude Desktop is open, and by default it asks before permanently deleting any files.
Try: "Organize my Downloads folder by file type and date."
Schedule recurring work
Ask Claude to run a task on a schedule, like a summary of your inbox every Monday morning. Scheduled tasks can run in the cloud, so they keep going when your computer is off. Learn more in
Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork
.
Try: "Every weekday at 8 AM, summarize new messages in my team's Slack channels."
Check in from your phone
A task you start at your desk shows up in Claude Mobile too, so you can see how it's going, answer questions from Claude, and redirect the work from anywhere. You can also start a task from your phone, and Claude keeps working in the cloud.
Make Claude your own
Skills:
Teach Claude how you like a task done, and it follows those steps whenever the task comes up. Learn more in
Use skills in Claude
.
Plugins:
Add plugins that bundle skills and connectors for your role. Learn more in
Use plugins in Claude
.
Choose how much Claude checks with you
A permission setting in the message box controls how independently Claude works:
Auto (default on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans):
Claude keeps working without stopping to ask about each step, and automated safety checks run before it takes an action.
Manual (default on Enterprise plans):
Claude asks before it takes actions, and you choose whether to allow each one.
You can change the setting at any time, and you can stop or redirect Claude while it works. The setting applies to the whole conversation. For work with real consequences, like sending messages or changing important files, stay close and review what Claude does. Learn more in
Use Claude Cowork safely
.
Pick up where you left off
One conversation list:
Your quick questions and longer tasks live together in
Recents
.
Memory:
Claude uses what it remembers from your chats in the tasks it works on for you.
Projects:
Keep files, instructions, and context together for related work. Projects work in every conversation.
Instructions for Claude:
Set preferences that apply to every conversation in
Settings > Your Claude
(or
Settings > Account
in the older Settings layout).
What happened to Claude Cowork?
In the new experience, everything Claude Cowork does is available from any conversation. Your existing Cowork tasks, projects, connectors, skills, artifacts, and files carry over, and those Cowork tasks open as they did before, so you can continue them. The model picker and the “Code” tab are where they were.
What's in a new place
Cowork tasks:
Together with your chats in
Recents
.
Global instructions:
The Cowork
Global instructions
setting is now part of
Instructions for Claude
in
Settings > Your Claude
(or
Settings > Account
in the older Settings layout). Check that your instructions are what you want.
Web search:
There's no web search toggle. Claude searches the web when it helps.
Research:
Type /deep-research, or click the “+” button below the chat input, then choose “Research.”
Files:
Files Claude creates appear alongside the conversation. In Claude Desktop, the folder Cowork saved its work to is still there. Look for
Storage folder
in
Settings
. Folders you gave Cowork access to are listed under
Trusted folders
.
Memory from local tasks:
Memory from Cowork tasks that ran only on your computer stays with those tasks.
Current limitations
Add from GitHub
isn't supported.
Branching a conversation
from an earlier point isn't available.
Incognito chats
still work, but they open in the previous experience, so Claude can't create files or run code in them.
Search
doesn't include older Cowork tasks. It covers your chats and new conversations, and you can still find older tasks by name in
Recents
.
Dispatch
isn't available to new users. If you already use Dispatch, you can keep using it for now. Learn more in
Assign tasks from anywhere in Claude Cowork
.
How usage works
Everything you do with Claude counts toward your plan's usage limits.  Longer agentic tasks that search the web, run code, or create files generally use more than a quick question. While the new experience rolls out, usage may be measured slightly differently for accounts that have it and accounts that don’t. Check your current usage in
Settings > Usage
, and learn more in
Usage limit best practices
.
Get started
Open Claude and describe what you need, the way you'd brief a colleague. You'll get better results when you include:
Your desired outcome:
what you want to end up with, like "a one-page summary" or "a spreadsheet with a tab for each region."
The format:
how you want the result delivered, like a Word document, a slide deck, or a message you can paste into Slack.
Inputs Claude will need:
the files, links, or apps Claude should work from.
Not sure where to start? Ask Claude what it can help with.

One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job. The node may pass basic health checks and show normal utilization, leaving operators to discover the problem only after the workload is running.
These issues can appear at any point in a cluster’s lifecycle. A GPU cluster that passes readiness checks at handover changes as nodes are replaced, drivers are patched, and capacity is added. Without repeated validation, the original certification no longer reflects the cluster’s condition.
This visibility gap wastes compute on failing nodes and leaves healthy nodes idle out of caution. Utilization metrics can mask these losses. Goodput, which is the volume of work successfully completed, provides a more useful measure of cluster efficiency. Maintaining cluster readiness requires validation throughout the cluster’s operational lifecycle—after configuration changes, as capacity grows, and before repaired nodes return to service.
The
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform
brings together technologies for designing, building, and operating efficient, resilient AI factories. Its open source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, includes tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.
Configure
: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) establishes a reproducible baseline for GPU-optimized Kubernetes infrastructure.
Defines version-locked configuration recipes for components such as networking, storage, and drivers.
Renders recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools.
Certify

Tests GPUs, networking, and storage using AI workloads and diagnostics.
Records certification results and helps identify faulty nodes.
Operate

Publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health.
When configured, cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, and remediates faults.
Can trigger revalidation with NVCRE before nodes return to service.
All three are open source projects licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions.
Before you begin, install and configure
AICR
,
NVCRE
, and
NVSentinel
using their installation guides. The examples assume access to a Kubernetes GPU cluster with the required CLIs, controllers, dependencies, and NVCRE test provider configured.
This walkthrough follows one cluster through its lifecycle: configuration from a recipe, certification before production use, monitoring during operation, and recertification after repair. Each command is a step in that sequence.
Configure: A baseline you can reproduce
AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version-controlled files and renders them into artifacts your existing deployment tooling applies. It generates and validates; your deployer applies and reconciles them. Declarative templates help detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs.
You describe the target environment. AICR resolves it against a library of validated overlays and emits a recipe:
aicr recipe --service eks --accelerator h100 --os ubuntu \
--intent inference --platform dynamo -o recipe.yaml
Each component entry in the resulting recipe pins a version and declares which dependencies must be healthy before the component is installed:
apiVersion: aicr.run/v1alpha2
componentRefs:
- name: dynamo-platform
chart: dynamo-platform
namespace: dynamo-system
source: https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia/ai-dynamo
type: Helm
version: 1.4.2
valuesFile: components/dynamo-platform/values.yaml
dependencyRefs:
- grove
- cert-manager
- kube-prometheus-stack
- gpu-operator
- kai-scheduler
The recipe includes three key properties:
Pinned versions:
The version is fixed, helping you reproduce the software configuration and investigate failures. In contrast, a floating tag can point to a different software version over time, making failures harder to reproduce.
A dependency graph:
dependencyRefs
declares what must be installed and healthy first. AICR resolves the graph when it renders the bundle, so the ordering is already encoded in the artifacts your deployer applies. You don’t need to specify that cert-manager comes before NVSentinel, and adding a component later doesn’t require renumbering.
Health assertions per component:
Each entry carries a
healthCheckAsserts
block that runs after installation and checks whether the component meets its configured health criteria. Kubernetes can report a pod stuck in
CrashLoopBackOff
as
Running
, so a check based only on the pod phase can miss a broken component. The shipped assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone.
Rendering the recipe is a separate step that connects AICR to your existing pipeline:
aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles
--deployer
accepts
helm
,
argocd
,
argocd-helm
,
flux
, or
helmfile
, so the same validated recipe becomes Argo CD
Application
manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands. You can keep your existing deployment tooling and use AICR to generate its configuration artifacts.
Because the recipe is a file, you can use version history, code review, and drift detection to manage the baseline.
# Check a live cluster against the recipe's constraints
aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml
# Compare a golden baseline against the live cluster, non-zero exit on drift
aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift
--fail-on-drift
turns the drift check into a continuous integration (CI) gate rather than a report.
Certify: Prove the cluster will run the job
The cluster is now built to a known baseline. It still needs workload validation. Standard health checks confirm that basic services are running. They don’t confirm that the cluster can run a demanding multinode job across its interconnect without stalling. NVCRE validates workload readiness by running training jobs and NVIDIA Collective Communication Library
(NCCL)
tests.
NVSentinel manages validation requests, scheduling gates, quarantine, and repair, while NVCRE runs tests and records results. Table 1 shows how these responsibilities fit into the node validation lifecycle.
Step

for new or repaired nodes. After upgrades or fabric changes, operators cordon the nodes and create the request.

nvcre-provider

3. Record and evaluate

Certification
resource. The lifecycle manager evaluates the results.
The validation outcome determines whether the scheduling gate can be removed.
4. Resolve the gate

A certification identifies the nodes to test, the categories to run, and the thresholds that determine whether the tests pass or fail:
apiVersion: nvcre.nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: Certification
metadata:
name: gpu-cluster-cert
spec:
target:
nodeSelector:
nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true"
categories:
- domain: communication
variant: nccl-all-reduce
- domain: training
variant: nemotron5-8b
options:
thresholds:
busBandwidthGBps: "value >= 300"
nvcrectl certification run --cert-file certification.yaml --wait
nvcrectl certification report gpu-cluster-cert -n <namespace>
The report shows each category’s status, runtime, measured bandwidth, and the reason for any failed nodes.
Thresholds make certification a performance gate. None are configured by default. Without the
options.thresholds
block above, a run reports its measurements and fails when the tests can’t start. A node performing below the target can pass. Thresholds help catch performance degradation rather than breakage.
The catalog covers NCCL communication variants, the NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) level 4 diagnostic suite, and pretraining workloads using NVIDIA NeMo Framework with 8-billion- and 56-billion-parameter models. A
WorkloadRun
resource turns your own containerized test into a certification check. NVCRE infers the rest from the target nodes, so the manifest stays concise on any supported platform.
These tests can help identify performance issues that aren’t apparent in telemetry. A GPU running just below its performance target might not produce Xid errors, breach monitoring thresholds, or cause node metrics to appear abnormal. That one GPU can slow a synchronous training job to its slowest rank, and operators may find out hours later, or only after a user complains. An NCCL bandwidth test can uncover this performance degradation.
Isolating the cause matters as much. If a 64-node all-reduce yields poor bandwidth, every node is suspect, and bisecting by hand can be time-consuming. NVCRE splits failing groups and reruns the tests until it reaches a minimum group size, then reports the suspect nodes with a reason for each.
Run NVCRE before handing a cluster or new capacity to a tenant and when repaired hardware rejoins the pool.
Operate: Detection and remediation under load
The certified cluster is now running workloads and needs to stay healthy. AICR and NVCRE provide point-in-time validation. NVSentinel runs continuously alongside workloads.
NVSentinel watches signals the cluster already produces: DCGM health checks, Xid errors, network interface card (NIC) states, and cloud provider maintenance events. It doesn’t consume GPU time, leaving GPUs available for workloads.
NVSentinel installs in monitoring mode by default: it reports faults as node conditions and won’t cordon, evict, or remediate nodes. You can roll it out on a live cluster while you evaluate its reports. You can enable quarantine, draining, and remediation once you trust the reported signals.
Detection publishes a health event; a Fault Quarantine ruleset decides what happens to the node. Rulesets use Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions in your values file:
fault-quarantine:
ruleSets:
- enabled: true
version: "1"
name: "GPU fatal error ruleset"
priority: 100
match:
all:
- kind: "HealthEvent"
expression: "event.agent == 'gpu-health-monitor' && event.componentClass == 'GPU' && event.isFatal == true"
- kind: "Node"
expression: |
!('k8saas.nvidia.com/ManagedByNVSentinel' in node.metadata.labels &&
node.metadata.labels['k8saas.nvidia.com/ManagedByNVSentinel'] == "false")
cordon:
shouldCordon: true
taint:
key: "nvidia.com/gpu-error"
value: "fatal"
effect: "NoSchedule"
A cordon or taint provides a signal that your scheduler, alerting, and lifecycle tooling can use without integrating directly with NVSentinel.
A circuit breaker limits the impact by capping how many GPU nodes can be quarantined in a sliding window. The
Fault Quarantine configuration guide
covers the bounds and the rest of the ruleset options.

In an AI factory, high bandwidth memory (HBM)is the fastest, most expensive, and most contested memory tier. Every byte spent on a redundant weight copy, an idle session’s KV cache, or a recomputed prefix is a byte that is not being used to produce tokens. The question is no longer how much memory a GPU has, but how much useful work each byte delivers.
The generational data in Figure 1 below shows why. From GB300 to NVIDIA Rubin, capacity held at 288 GB while bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s.
agentic throughput per megawatt grew far faster. On
SemiAnalysis AgentX
, which replays recorded coding-agent sessions with real tool-call gaps and growing context, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 then delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user.
Figure 1. GPU throughput grew by 30x while HBM capacity remained approximately the same from GB300 NVL72 to Vera Rubin NVL72.
Capacity alone cannot explain a 30x gain delivered from the same 288 GB per GPU. The difference is how much useful work each byte delivers.
NVIDIA treats this as a co-design problem that spans GPU architecture, the scale-up interconnect, serving software, the CPU, and storage. This post examines five ways that co-design maximizes the value of each byte of memory, from the bits that encode a single weight to the shared storage that preserves and reuses context across agentic turns and nodes.
1. How does NVFP4 store more intelligence in fewer bytes?
The most direct way to raise the value of a byte is to make each value smaller without losing what it encodes.
NVFP4
does this with a 4-bit E2M1 element and two levels of scaling: Every 16-value micro-block shares an FP8 (E4M3) scale factor, and a per-tensor FP32 scale sits on top. The result is a format that is small enough to free significant HBM, yet granular enough to preserve accuracy where naive 4-bit formats fall short.
Figure 2. NVFP4 combines 4-bit values with block-level and tensor-level scaling.
Applied to weights, NVFP4 reduces the model footprint by approximately 3.5x relative to FP16 and 1.8x relative to FP8, freeing memory for what agentic inference needs most: more KV-cache capacity, larger batches, and higher concurrency. NVFP4 has become the default precision for open agentic benchmarks with strict accuracy requirements, including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX, and MLPerf Endpoints. Across these benchmarks and leading mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, it delivers up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline at the same interactivity (Figure 3 below).
Figure 3. NVFP4 delivers 4x the throughput per megawatt of FP8 at the same interactivity for DeepSeek R1 on GB300.
The same principle extends to the KV cache itself.
NVFP4 KV cache
cuts the cache footprint by up to 50% compared with FP8, so approximately 2x more context stays resident on device. Fewer evictions mean higher cache-hit rates during prefill, while a smaller cache means less bandwidth consumed during decode.
Figure 4. NVFP4 KV cache archives over 99% of BF16 baseline scores across 10 DeepSeek-v4-Pro benchmarks
NVFP4 shrinks the bytes. The next question is where those bytes live, and how many copies of them the AI factory has to keep.
2. How does the NVLink scale-up domain turn 72 GPUs into one memory pool?
MoE models activate only a subset of parameters per token, but every expert’s weights must still live somewhere in HBM. When experts are packed onto a small number of GPUs, each GPU spends a large share of its memory on weights, and each decode step pays a heavy weight-loading cost for the MoE GroupGEMMs. The bytes are resident, but they are not working hard.
Wide expert parallelism
(Wide-EP) in NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM changes that ratio by spreading experts across eight or more GPUs. With DeepSeek-R1 at EP64, each GPU holds four experts per layer, or 232 expert blocks across 58 MoE layers out of 14,848 in the full model. Fewer expert weights per GPU means:
Capacity:
More HBM per GPU is left for KV cache, larger batches, and higher concurrency.
Arithmetic intensity:
GroupGEMM kernels reuse each loaded weight across more tokens, raising FLOPs per byte.
Balance:
The Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB) redistributes hot and cold experts between forward passes, so no GPU’s memory is overcommitted while another sits idle.
Figure 5. GB300 NVL72 delivers 10x the token throughput per megawatt of H200 NVL8 at 100 tokens per second per user.
This only works because the scale-up domain makes remote bytes nearly as useful as local ones. Every MoE layer triggers all-to-all dispatch and combine traffic, and without a high-bandwidth fabric, those collectives would erase the gains. On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs that traffic, and large EP (EP32) delivers up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than small EP (EP8) at 100 tokens per second per user.
Vera Rubin NVL72 extends the same design point. Each Rubin GPU brings up to 288 GB of HBM4 and 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, for roughly 20.7 TB of HBM4 across the rack. Rubin also adds inline memory tensor acceleratory (TMA) descriptor updates, so one shared descriptor can serve every expert with a common layout, reducing the metadata overhead that grows with expert count.
Wide-EP decides where weight bytes live. The next lever decides whether KV cache bytes, once computed, are ever computed again.
3. How does NVIDIA Dynamo make every cached byte count?
The key-value (KV) cache stores intermediate attention calculations from previously processed tokens so the model can reuse them instead of recomputing them. This inference state is ephemeral and can be evicted and recomputed when needed, but KV cache is only valuable if it is reused. Agentic workloads are full of reuse opportunities: system prompts, tool schemas, shared documents, and the growing history of a multistep task. But if a request lands on a GPU that does not hold its prefix, or if that prefix was evicted moments earlier, the system pays for prefill again. The bytes existed; they were just in the wrong place.
NVIDIA Dynamo
is the distributed serving layer that closes this gap. It treats KV cache as a fleet-wide resource rather than a per-GPU side effect, and it does so through three co-designed capabilities:
KV-aware routing:
The Dynamo router tracks where KV blocks reside and considers both cached-prefix overlap and worker load when placing requests. It balances existing context against the cost of sending work to an utilized GPU and turns potential recomputations into cache hits.
Disaggregated serving:
Prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, each sized for its own compute and memory profile. Decode GPUs can dedicate HBM to KV cache and batch size rather than reserving headroom for bursty prefill.
KV Cache Runner (KVCR):
This tracks where every block lives across configured GPU, pinned CPU, and storage tiers, including local SSDs and mounted network filesystems. A prefix preserved outside HBM can be restored when a later request needs it, allowing useful context to survive GPU eviction and continue saving prefill work. KVCR uses the
NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL)
for its storage-transfer paths, allowing cached blocks to move while the GPU processes other work. KVCR also enables distributed reuse, with router-provided hints helping a selected worker retrieve cached context from a peer, while the inference engine retains control of GPU memory and local host offloading. The additional KVCR-Guard feature preserves committed KVCR-managed host-memory cache across an engine failure as long as the guard service and host remain available.
Figure 6. Dynamo combines KV-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and tiered KV cache reuse.
Dynamo’s KV-cache offloading depends on fast retrieval: Preserving a prefix outside HBM saves time when loading it is faster than repeating prefill. NIXL connects this offloading path to external storage systems. In separate validation tests, storage vendors VAST Data and WEKA demonstrated 35 GB/s to one H100 GPU using GPUDirect Storage and up to 270 GB/s of aggregate read throughput across eight H100 GPUs through a custom NIXL plugin, respectively. These tests showed that external storage could supply KV cache to the tested GPU systems without becoming the transfer bottleneck, supporting cache capacity beyond HBM. A separate VAST test demonstrated the response-time benefit: Using vLLM and LMCache on a DGX H100 system, loading stored KV cache instead of recomputing it reduced time to first token for Qwen3-32B with a 130K-token prompt.
Dynamo coordinates where cached bytes go and when they come back. The next two levers expand the capacity available for that context, starting with CPU memory.
4. How does the NVIDIA Vera CPU keep idle context from wasting HBM?
Agentic inference does not run in one uninterrupted pass. A single session alternates between GPU model steps and CPU-side work: tool calls, code execution, retrieval, database queries, and sandboxed evaluation. During each of those gaps, any session KV cache retained in HBM occupies capacity without serving active token generation, while other requests compete for the same bytes.
Figure 7. Faster tool calls on Vera keep the KV cache in HBM, avoiding rebuilding and starting the next model step sooner.
In a fully subscribed AI factory, the GPU does not wait. It takes on new requests while the tool call runs, and the longer the gap, the more likely the original session’s KV cache is evicted to make room. When the tool returns, the GPU may have to rebuild that context through a full prefill rather than resume from a cached state. A slow CPU therefore costs HBM twice: first as idle residency, then as recomputation.
The
NVIDIA Vera CPU
attacks both sides of this problem:
Shorter gaps:
88 Olympus cores deliver 1.8x faster single-threaded performance, 40% lower peak loaded latency than x86 CPUs, and up to 14 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core. Faster, more predictable tool calls shrink the window in which KV cache is exposed to eviction pressure.
A fast place to park context:
Each Vera CPU provides up to 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X, more than 5x the HBM4 capacity of a single Rubin GPU. NVIDIA NVLink-C2C connects it coherently to Rubin at 1.8 TB/s, roughly 7x the 256 GB/s of an x16 PCIe Gen 6 link.
Together, these capabilities change the economics of an idle session. Instead of holding its KV cache in HBM or discarding it, Dynamo’s KV Block Manager can stage it in Vera memory for the duration of the tool call and bring it back over NVLink-C2C when the agent resumes. HBM stays dedicated to sessions that are actively generating tokens, and the paused session avoids paying for prefill twice.
Figure 8. Vera Rubin offloads inactive KV caches to host memory, freeing GPU HBM for active sessions.
Vera memory is the warm tier, sized for context that will return within a turn. For context that must survive across turns, agents, and nodes, the AI factory needs a tier that is larger still.
5. How does NVIDIA CMX extend context memory across the pod?
Keeping every reusable KV-cache byte in GPU or host memory limits capacity for active inference, but discarding it can force recomputation.. Multi-turn sessions, long-horizon tasks, and multi-agent workflows that share working memory all generate KV cache that will be needed again, often minutes later and often on a different node. Longer context windows and more concurrent sessions increase KV-cache capacity requirements beyond GPU HBM (G1 in Figure 9 below) and host memory (G2). The traditional hierarchy was not designed for this data. Local SSDs (G3) are bound to one node, while shared enterprise storage (G4) is built for durable data and carries replication and metadata overhead that ephemeral KV cache does not need.
NVIDIA CMX
context memory storage closes this gap with a new G3.5 tier: Ethernet-attached flash, shared at the pod level, and optimized specifically for KV cache. It is built on the NVIDIA STX reference design and co-designed across four layers:
Storage processing:
The NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor manages the NVMe SSDs, runs storage services, and offloads KV-cache data movement, data integrity and encryption. Its integrated NVIDIA Vera CPU accelerates CPU-side storage processing, extending the same CPU architecture used for agent execution into the storage data path.
Networking
: NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet provides low-latency, high-bandwidth RDMA access between compute nodes and CMX storage nodes.
KV-aware services:
NVIDIA DOCA Memos provides KV-aware services and I/O control on BlueField-4, treating context as a first-class resource for placement and sharing.
Serving integration:
Dynamo and NIXL make CMX appear as one seamless context tier across the pod, prestaging context and routing requests to where KV cache already resides.
Figure 9. NVIDIA CMX adds a shared G3.5 tier for pod-wide KV-cache capacity and reuse
The pod-level design is what raises the value of each byte. A prefix computed once on one node can be reused across compatible model instances in the pod, so agents that share documents, tools, or working memory can avoid duplicate prefill. Pooling context storage across the pod reduces KV-cache duplication and stranded capacity across nodes, extending effective GPU memory for inference. By prestaging reusable context into GPU or host memory, CMX reduces inference stalls, while its KV-cache-optimized storage tier lowers the power overhead of serving that context. Together, these capabilities help CMX deliver up to 5x higher tokens per second and up to 5x better power efficiency compared with traditional storage for long-context inference.
How do the five levers work together?
Each lever removes a different kind of waste. NVFP4 removes bits a value does not need, Wide-EP removes redundant weight copies, Dynamo removes recomputation, Vera removes idle residency during tool calls, and CMX enables KV-cache sharing and reuse across nodes. Because these levers are designed as one memory system, not as independent parts, the gains stack: A 4-bit KV block saves space in HBM, in Vera memory, and in CMX alike.
The result is an AI factory that measures memory not by capacity alone, but by the useful tokens each byte produces. Vera Rubin NVL72 shows what that looks like: up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72, from the same 288 GB per GPU. As agentic workloads grow, every byte counts.

items.title: Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels Per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep
items.content:
Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels
- Google Developers Blog
Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels
NOV. 3, 2026
Sergio Villani
Technical Solutions
Google Cloud AI
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep climbing. Price per million tokens isn't the metric that actually governs production economics anymore. The dominating metric is now cost per successful task: total spend across every loop iteration, tool call, retry and internal thinking pass divided by the number of tasks that pass verification.
When an agent calls a high-thinking reasoning configuration for every micro-decision in its harness, you're paying deep-reasoning prices for questions a lightweight configuration already answers accurately. To prevent this unnecessary overhead, consider adding a lightweight routing layer that can intercept routine decisions before they ever reach an expensive reasoning model.
That is the premise behind wiring TypeSafe's Jev classifier in front of Google Antigravity's model calls. Rather than generating text token by token, Jev—a specialized structured-output classifier designed for high-throughput decision pipelines—evaluates structured classification primitives in a single forward pass: a Choice from a list, a numeric Score or a Noul, which returns a 0 to 1 probability for a binary statement.
For full disclosure, Google has no partnership with TypeSafe, and this article is not an endorsement of TypeSafe or its products. Jev is used here as one example of a lightweight classifier, and the same routing pattern can be built with other classifiers, including Google-native ones. The
Getting started with discriminative models
codelab, for example, runs the same kind of classifier on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, in your own Google Cloud project.
We ran a 50-question, auto-graded, coding-agent benchmark against live Gemini and Jev APIs to test whether a near-free classifier can route each task to the cheapest model that still gets it right. Here's what we learned:
1. Regex and token-length harness routers collapse on unseen agent tasks
The naive way to ask Jev to route a coding task is a single broad Choice question:
simple
or
complex
. When we tested that first on 16 coding-agent tasks, Jev routed nearly everything to
simple
, even tasks requiring an LRU cache trace or modular exponentiation. TypeSafe's documentation warns against this exact anti-pattern. If a question weighs multiple factors or requires a meta-judgment, decompose it into an atomic check.
When we replaced the broad Choice question with one atomic Noul question, it fixed the separation immediately. The question was: does answering this require performing more than one sequential calculation, simulation step or logical deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format check or one-step classification?
def call_jev(question_text):
body = {
"state": question_text,
"model": "jev-latest",
"questions": {
"multi_step": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": (
"Answering this requires performing more than one "
"sequential calculation, simulation step, or logical "
"deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format "
"check, or one-step classification."
),
}
},
}
# Send the request above to the classifier's API.
# response.answers["multi_step"].noul is the probability used to route.
Python
Copied
On those initial 16 tasks, Jev routed 13 of 16 in agreement with our hand-labeled difficulty on the first run and 14 of 16 on the second pass. Many engineering teams ask whether they even need a classifier API when they can write a zero-cost regex and prompt-length heuristic in Python, matching words like
sequence
,
modulo
and
race condition
or escalating any prompt over 35 words.
On the 16 development questions used to write those exact rules, the local heuristic scored 15 of 16, or 93.8%. To test whether that heuristic survived contact with realistic coding-agent traffic, we froze its code without changing a character and added 34 unseen held-out tasks across seven coding-agent buckets: fact extraction, schema validation, short classification, single-hop code checks, state simulation traces, math or logic chains and subtle language-semantics bugs.
On the 34 held-out questions, the frozen heuristic dropped 23.2 percentage points to 70.6%. Realistic simple tasks such as extracting a port from a Kubernetes YAML manifest, a file path from a unified git diff header or a line number from a Python traceback exceeded 35 words and triggered false escalations. Conversely, concise multi-step code traces such as mutable default arguments across calls, Python dictionary key hashing on
{1: "a", True: "b", 1.0: "c"}
and C short-circuit evaluation lacked the heuristic's hardcoded puzzle words and were falsely routed to the simple path. Jev classified all 34 unseen tasks with 100.0% agreement, 34 of 34, reaching 48 of 50, or 96.0%, across the full suite.
2. MaxOutputTokens is a ceiling, not a thinking-budget dial
A common mistake when building a fast-path router is assuming that setting a low maxOutputTokens cap on a reasoning model will make it spend less on easy tasks. Our 50-question data shows why that assumption fails.
When we compared
gemini-3.8-flash
with
maxOutputTokens=300
against
gemini-3.8-flash
with
maxOutputTokens=4096
while leaving
thinkingConfig
at the API default, both configurations spent almost identical thinking tokens on the 27 tasks Jev labeled
SIMPLE
:
Note:
Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.
Capping the model's output at 300 tokens didn't save any money on easy tasks. The cap is only a ceiling, and easy answers never came close to it. On the easy tasks, the capped version actually cost slightly more than the uncapped one. All the cap did was break 7 of the 25 hard tasks. On six of them, the model ran out of room while still reasoning and never gave an answer. On the seventh, it squeezed its reasoning to fit, finished on time and got the answer wrong.
So a Jev router that sends easy tasks to the capped model and hard ones to normal Flash got all 50 right. It still cost slightly more than skipping the router and using normal Flash for everything, and it was slower. If your cheap option doesn't actually make the model think less on easy tasks, no router can save you money. Not even a perfect one that costs nothing.
3. Benchmark Jev against the strongest setup without a router
The obvious way to spend less on thinking is to ask the model to think less. So we ran a second round of tests with two lighter options: Flash-Lite, which doesn't think at all by default, and Gemini 3.8 Flash with its thinking level set to low. We added those results to the same results file, matched question by question.
A note on timing. Most of the router's time per task is spent in Flash-Lite and Flash calls, which we measured in the same run and time window as the plain Flash baseline, so the speed comparison between them is fair. Jev's own decision is a small share of the total and comes from the first round. Speed comparisons against default Flash or Pro mix the two rounds, so read those as approximate.
Note
: Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.
The 7-bucket breakdown shows where
gemini-3.5-flash-lite
and the heuristic router missed tasks and how
Router Jev: Flash-Lite to 3.8 LOW
recovered 100% accuracy:
The strongest setup without a router was Gemini 3.8 Flash on low thinking. It solved all 50 tasks. That's the number a router had to beat.
The Jev router beat it.
It sends every task to Flash-Lite first and escalates only what Jev flags as complex. It also solved all 50 tasks, and it can help reduce both cost and response time compared with running low thinking on everything. On prompts this short the cost difference per task is small, so for an interactive agent the shorter wait is the bigger benefit.
Why it works.
On its own, Flash-Lite answered every simple task in half a second but missed 6 of the 25 hard ones. Jev flagged all 6 as complex with high confidence and escalated them. That brought its cost close to what a perfect router would achieve.
The keyword heuristic was cheaper
, but only because it got things wrong. It sent 5 hard tasks to Flash-Lite, and 2 of them failed, for 48 of 50.
Escalating to a heavier setting didn't pay here
. Routing hard tasks to Flash on default thinking was cheaper than running default thinking everywhere. It still cost more than running low thinking on everything, which already solved all 50. A heavier escalation target only makes sense when the low setting starts failing.
Limits: one run per setup, 50 prompts with hand-assigned difficulty and simple automatic grading.
4. Price per token doesn't tell the whole story
Two things in our results only show up once you look past it.
Routing and caching pull in opposite directions.
Our test prompts were short, standalone tasks, and on those the Jev router helped reduce both cost and response time. Real coding agents often look different. They send the same big block of context on every turn, such as a map of the repository and the tool definitions. Agent Platform Context Caching stores that block so you pay 75% to 90% less to resend it. The catch is that a cache belongs to one model. If your agent switches between Flash-Lite and Flash from turn to turn, it either keeps two caches or loses the discount. The practical split: route short, self-contained tasks like log parsing or schema checks, and keep long, context-heavy turns on one model.
Match the model to the workload.
Gemini 3.1 Pro is built for deep, multi-step reasoning, and it brings that same depth to every request, including short lookups that don't need it. For a workload made mostly of quick checks and extractions, a Flash configuration is the better fit, and Pro is best saved for the tasks that need its reasoning depth. Model configurations can also apply different safety settings to security-related prompts. In our run, the Pro configuration declined two short code-security review prompts that Flash answered. If your agent performs security reviews, test those prompts on the configuration you plan to use.
Cost per successful task needs the right denominator
Other ways to build the router.
Jev is one way to get a fast classifier, but not the only one. The
Getting started with discriminative models
codelab runs the same Choice, Score and Noul questions on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, hosted on a Compute Engine GPU VM or on Cloud Run in your own Google Cloud project. An open-source server exposes the same API in front of it, so the routing code in this article only needs a different endpoint. Our results come from Jev, so measure accuracy and latency on your own tasks before switching, and keep in mind that a self-hosted model is billed by the GPU-hour rather than by the token.
Taken together, the results give three practical rules.
Start with Flash on low thinking before you build a router.
It solved all 50 tasks and cost considerably less than the default setting. Lowering the output token limit is not a substitute, because it doesn't reduce how much the model thinks on easy tasks. Set the thinking level directly, with thinkingLevel: "LOW".
Use Jev to route short, standalone tasks.
Send simple tasks to Flash-Lite and hard ones to Flash on low thinking. Ask Jev one simple yes-or-no question per factor. In our test, this helped reduce cost and response time compared with running Flash on low thinking for everything, and came close to what a perfect router would achieve. Keep long, context-heavy turns on a single model so caching keeps working. For high-volume warehouse workloads,
Jeff Nelson's BigQuery and Cloud Run cascade pattern
applies the same idea.
Measure what your agent actually spends.
Send your agent's traces and thinking-token counts to Cloud Logging and BigQuery, so you can see which tasks drive your spend and catch truncation or retries that inflate it. The benchmark code will be published after open-source review.
In summary, the most cost-effective way to run an agent is to match each task to the model that fits it.
Start with a fast model on a light setting. You'll often find it already gets the job done. Then add a small, almost free classifier like Jev to send only the hard tasks to a stronger model, and ask simple yes-or-no questions rather than one broad one. Judge every option by what it costs per task done right, not per token.

items.title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents See Google A2Ui in action! Learn how to natively render agentic UIs across Langchain, AWS Strands, Microsoft agents, and Goog
items.content:
Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
- Google Developers Blog
Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
OCT. 29, 2026
Google A2UI Team
Atai Barkai
CEO at CopilotKit
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Agent-User Interactions are now evolving from text exchanges to rich UIs. Until recently, most conversations looked like this:
User:
"Find me a holiday package to Bali in March."
Agent:
(six packages in prose, each with dates, hotel, flights, price)
User:
"The five-night one with breakfast."
Agent:
"Here's the link. You can book it on the operator's site."
Agents could plan the trip, but everything came back as walls of text. They had no standard way to render a selectable list of packages, a map of the destinations, or a date picker to carry you through the rest of the booking, inside the conversation itself.
Generative UI is the layer that lets agents build interfaces at runtime, shaped by what each request needs - giving users a rich, interactive experience. Implementing that takes two pieces: a way to describe the UI and an agentic stack that connects your agent to your application and renders that UI.
A2UI (Agent-to-UI)
is Google's framework-agnostic open standard for Generative UI. The agent describes an interface as data, and your application draws it with the components you already have. It's transport-agnostic by design.
CopilotKit
provides the agent-integration stack to integrate with agent frameworks like “LangChain”, “AWS Strands”, “Google ADK”, etc. for building user-facing agentic apps. It provides a toolkit for building rich applications with A2UI protocol, including the chat surface, runtime, and leverages A2UI renderer, across React and Angular. CopilotKit also provides custom A2UI renderers for Vue and Slack.
What is A2UI?
Generative UI covers a spectrum of approaches, from using predefined higher order components, to enabling your AI agent to have the flexibility to decide how to build the UI.
At the controlled end, you build each component ahead of time, and the agent picks which one to render and with what data. It's brand-safe but it does not allow for deep customization and personalization based on the user’s intent. At the open end, the agent returns a raw UI program written in HTML, Javascript and/or Dart that renders inside a sandboxed iframe. That covers anything you did not plan for, at the cost of a surface that drifts from your design system and executes code a model wrote.
A2UI
works through the entire spectrum. It participates in
controlled generation with decision models
like Typesafe’s Jev and also open-ended code generation that may output A2UI JSON messages. The declarative mode, where agents assemble pre-declared components and functions, is the most popular. A2UI is the framework-agnostic standard for declaring UI intent, so local or remote agents can generate your UI from your existing component catalog using a common language.
Security first.
A2UI is a declarative data format rather than executable code. The client keeps a catalog of trusted components, so anything the agent invents outside that set is caught before it reaches the screen.
LLM-friendly and streaming.
The payload is a flat list of small JSON messages that reference each other by ID, so the agent emits it incrementally and the client renders components as they arrive.
Framework-agnostic and portable.
The same response renders through
React, Lit, Angular, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose (Android) or Flutter
(multi-platform), and through
community renderers
for Vue, or even the terminal.
Frontend developers can now ship the building blocks once, and the agent composes them for each request.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
The
Basic Catalog
ships 18 general-purpose primitives across layout, display, input, and containers. The agent can compose entirely different interfaces from the same 18 primitives, depending on what the request needs.
The Basic Catalog is deliberately sparse, so most production apps
define their own custom catalog
. A custom component can be anything your frontend already renders, including a live map the agent fills with coordinates while your renderer draws the route.
How A2UI and CopilotKit work together
CopilotKit is built on
AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol)
, which supports A2UI payload and provides Agent SDKs across many agentic backends.
Your agent emits A2UI operations. AG-UI carries them to the client as typed events. When the user takes any action, the values are sent back along the same stream.
A2UI works with any AG-UI compatible agent.
Frameworks like Google ADK, LangChain, Mastra and Strands are all AG-UI compatible, so the setup is identical whichever one your agent runs on.
Setting up A2UI in your app
Setup comes down to two things: connecting your agent to CopilotKit, and defining which components the agent is allowed to use.
Using Google ADK as the example, the
ag_ui_adk
package wraps any ADK agent and serves it as an AG-UI endpoint on FastAPI:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from ag_ui_adk import ADKAgent, add_adk_fastapi_endpoint
root_agent = LlmAgent(
name="flight_agent",
model="gemini-3.8-flash",
instruction="Help users find and book flights. Call generate_a2ui to show results.",
)
adk_agent = ADKAgent(
adk_agent=root_agent,
app_name="flights",
user_id="demo_user",
use_in_memory_services=True,
)
app = FastAPI()
add_adk_fastapi_endpoint(app, adk_agent, path="/")
Python
Copied
On the app side, you register that endpoint with the CopilotKit runtime at
/api/copilotkit
. It's a few lines of standard setup, covered in the
Google ADK quickstart
, and it needs nothing A2UI-specific.
A2UI itself turns on from the client, where your components already are. Define what the agent is allowed to draw, map each definition to a renderer, and pass the catalog to the CopilotKit provider.
import { CopilotKit, CopilotChat } from '@copilotkit/react-core/v2';
import {
createCatalog,
type CatalogDefinitions,
type CatalogRenderers,
} from '@copilotkit/a2ui-renderer';
import { z } from 'zod';
const catalogDefinitions = {
FlightCard: {
description: 'A flight result with airline, times, and stops.',
props: z.object({
airline: z.string(),
departs: z.string(),
arrives: z.string(),
stops: z.number(),
}),
},
} satisfies CatalogDefinitions;
const catalogRenderers = {
FlightCard: MyFlightCard, // your React component
} satisfies CatalogRenderers<typeof catalogDefinitions>;
const catalog = createCatalog(catalogDefinitions, catalogRenderers, {
catalogId: 'flight-catalog',
includeBasicCatalog: true,
});
<CopilotKit runtimeUrl="/api/copilotkit" a2ui={{ catalog }}>
<CopilotChat />
</CopilotKit>
JavaScript
Copied
The
description
goes into the agent's prompt, so the model knows when to reach for
FlightCard
instead of a generic card. The Zod schema validates the props it sends back.
The A2UI configuration can be set up ahead of time on the server, or it can be created dynamically, shipped from the client to the server with the request. The ADK code above used dynamic configuration which is why it used generate_a2ui without defining it. The
docs
cover both approaches.
That’s the CopilotKit path. You can also consume the event stream directly with
@ag-ui/client
and hand the A2UI operations to any compliant renderer:
@a2ui/react
, or the Flutter, Lit, or Angular equivalent.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Building bi-directional A2UI surfaces
Most agent-generated UI is one-shot. The agent draws something, you read it, and it goes stale the moment anything changes.
A2UI surfaces are bi-directional and the components are reactive
, which makes multi-step flows possible. Any action the user takes on the interface (picking dates, choosing a flight, entering passenger details) travels back along the same stream, and the agent re-emits the surface from there using those values.
Here is a high-level architecture example of an end-to-end booking flow, with an AG-UI agent on Cloud Run streaming A2UI surfaces to a CopilotKit frontend.
Two things make the round trip work: inputs bound to a data path, and a button carrying an action that names which paths to send back.
{ "id": "cabin", "component": "ChoicePicker", "variant": "mutuallyExclusive",
"options": [ { "label": "Economy", "value": "eco" },
{ "label": "Business", "value": "biz" } ],
"value": { "path": "/booking/cabin" } },
{ "id": "confirm", "component": "Button", "child": "confirm_label",
"action": { "event": { "name": "confirmBooking",
"context": { "cabin": { "path": "/booking/cabin" },
"email": { "path": "/booking/email" } } } } }
JSON
Copied
Validation runs on the client, so a bad email shows an error inline without a model call. Nothing reaches the agent until the button fires.
Then the client sends the bound values, and the agent re-emits against the same
surfaceId
. That is how the whole flow lives on one surface: flight search, results, passenger details, and confirmation.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Benefits of running A2UI over AG-UI
Every AG-UI integration inherets these benefits, so you don't have to build them yourself:
Minimal server-side setup:
the catalog reaches the agent on setup, so registering it on the client is all it takes.
Generation in a dedicated sub-agent:
the catalog and protocol rules stay out of your main agent's context window, and the surface streams to the client as the sub-agent produces it.
Self-healing output:
invalid generations are caught and the specific errors go back for a correction, so nothing broken reaches the screen.
Graceful failure:
when retries are exhausted, the surface resolves to a short message and the conversation continues instead of dying in an error state.
Get Started
Create a complete A2UI + CopilotKit application. This creates a starter A2UI application with Copilotkit Agent integration.
npx copilotkit@latest create --name my-app --framework a2ui
Shell
Copied
The
CopilotKit Dojo
has runnable A2UI demos: fixed server-side schema, dynamic schema against a custom catalog, and an error-recovery example where an invalid first render heals into a valid one.
A2UI Composer
CopilotKit A2UI Docs
Use A2UI with Any Agent Framework & Harness
Explore how to build Generative UI Agents with
CopilotKit
, or dive into
A2UI documentation
to learn how to integrate A2UI with any framework of your choice.
